title: Democracy & Its Variants
description: Liberal, illiberal, parliamentary, presidential: typologies of democratic rule

concepts.title: Defining Democracy: Procedural and Substantive
concepts.contentHtml:
"Democracy" covers a wide spread of regimes, so comparative politics has to settle what it's comparing before it compares anything.

In Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), the economist Joseph Schumpeter offered a deliberately minimalist procedural definition. For him, democracy is the institutional arrangement in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote.1 The bar is contested elections that turn over power, and popular happiness or social justice don't enter into it. Robert Dahl's influential expansion (Polyarchy, 1971) added the operational conditions Schumpeter took for granted: free and fair elections, broad suffrage, freedom of expression, alternative information sources, associational autonomy, and inclusive citizenship.

Critics on the left have argued that procedural democracy is necessary but not sufficient. Substantive definitions add that genuine democracy requires the social conditions (education, basic security, rough material equality, an independent press) that make political equality real rather than nominal. Most working scholars use a procedural core and a substantive horizon, and the disagreement is about how much of the latter has to be present before you'd call a regime democratic at all.

concepts.title: Liberal vs Illiberal Democracy
concepts.contentHtml:
Journalist Fareed Zakaria's 1997 essay "The Rise of Illiberal Democracy" named a phenomenon that has become central to comparative politics. Liberal democracy combines competitive elections with liberal components: constitutional limits on government power, independent courts, free press, protection of minorities, and individual rights. Illiberal democracy keeps the elections but discards the rest. Rulers win at the ballot box and then erode the institutions that constrain them.

The clearest contemporary cases are Hungary under Viktor Orbán (2010–2026) and Turkey under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Both won genuine majorities and then used them to capture courts, regulators, and most of the press. Orbán was nonetheless voted out in a 2026 landslide. The political scientist Steven Levitsky has called the broader pattern competitive authoritarianism, meaning regimes that hold elections but tilt the playing field so heavily that opposition victory becomes very difficult.

Ask how a democracy fails and the standard 20th-century answers are military coups and civil wars. In many countries those scripts have been replaced by gradual institutional erosion, which is why the category matters. Daniel Ziblatt and Levitsky's How Democracies Die (2018) catalogs the pattern. Democracies now usually fail through the steady capture of referees by elected leaders, with no single rupture.

concepts.title: Parliamentary, Presidential, and Semi-Presidential Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
Within liberal democracy, the biggest institutional choice is how the executive and the legislature relate to each other.

In a parliamentary system (UK, Germany, India, Japan, Israel, most of Europe), the prime minister and cabinet are drawn from the legislature and survive only as long as they command a parliamentary majority. Legislative and executive power are fused. Policy moves fast when the majority is solid, and governments turn over rapidly when it isn't.

In a presidential system (US, Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia, much of Latin America), the executive is elected separately and serves a fixed term independent of the legislature. Powers are separated, so lawmaking tends to be slower, divided government can bring gridlock, and executive tenure stays stable regardless of legislative confidence. The political scientist Juan Linz argued in "The Perils of Presidentialism" (1990) that fixed terms and dual democratic legitimacy make presidential systems prone to crisis when president and legislature deadlock.

A third family, semi-presidential systems (France since 1958, Russia, Romania, Portugal), combines an elected president with a prime minister responsible to parliament. The result is a hybrid. In periods of cohabitation, when president and parliamentary majority belong to different parties, who actually governs becomes a matter of ongoing institutional negotiation. Ask which system is "best" and there's no consensus; the comparative-politics literature has moved toward studying which combinations of institutions, party systems, and social cleavages produce stable democratic government.

title: Authoritarianism & Hybrid Regimes
description: Personalist, party-based, military, theocratic: how autocracies survive

concepts.title: Types of Authoritarian Regime
concepts.contentHtml:
Authoritarian regimes are at least as varied as democratic ones. The most influential modern typology, due to the political scientists Barbara Geddes, Joseph Wright, and Erica Frantz (How Dictatorships Work, 2018), distinguishes four main forms by who actually wields power.

Personalist regimes (Mobutu's Zaire, Saddam's Iraq, Putin's Russia in its current phase) concentrate power in a single ruler whose informal networks dominate the formal state. Single-party regimes (Soviet Union, China since 1949, Mexico's PRI for most of the 20th century) institutionalize power in a hegemonic party that selects leaders through internal procedures. Military regimes (juntas in Brazil 1964–1985, Argentina 1976–1983, Egypt under successive coups) are ruled by an officer corps as such, with the cabinet, courts, and parliament subordinated. Theocracies (Iran since 1979, the Taliban's Afghanistan) ground authority in religious office.

Each form has a different survival logic. Single-party regimes are durable but slow to reform. Military regimes are usually short-lived because officers prefer the barracks to politics. Personalist regimes survive as long as the leader does and often collapse afterwards. Theocracies are rare but very stable when established. The classification is imperfect, many regimes blend types, but it tracks meaningful differences in how repression, succession, and policy actually work.

concepts.title: How Autocracies Hold Power
concepts.contentHtml:
Authoritarian rulers face two threats: the public and their own elite. The literature distinguishes accordingly between repression (against ordinary citizens) and co-optation (of potential rivals).

Modern autocracies prefer co-optation where possible. Selectorate theory (Bueno de Mesquita and colleagues, 2003) models politics as the manipulation of a winning coalition: dictators reward a small inner circle of elites generously enough to keep them loyal, while spending little on the public. Patronage, oil revenues, control of state-owned companies, and rigged tenders are the typical vehicles. Selective inclusion (giving opposition figures parliamentary seats, ministry posts, or business deals) is cheaper than crushing them.

Repression remains a tool, but a graduated one. Most days, autocracies use surveillance, paperwork, regulatory harassment, selective tax enforcement, and the chilling effect on civil society. Mass repression is reserved for moments of acute threat: protest waves, suspected coups, ethnic mobilization. The political scientist Steven Levitsky and his colleagues have shown that the most durable autocracies are those that combine genuine elite cohesion with limited but credible repressive capacity.

concepts.title: Hybrid Regimes and the Gray Zone
concepts.contentHtml:
Many regimes today are neither fully democratic nor fully authoritarian. Hybrid regimes hold elections that are real but unfair, allow opposition that is real but constrained, and tolerate civil society that is real but harassed.

Levitsky and Way's category of competitive authoritarianism captures this gray zone: elections are competitive enough that the ruling party can sometimes lose, yet the playing field is tilted so heavily (through media control, abuse of state resources, intimidation, and selective rule of law) that genuine alternation is rare. Russia in the 2000s, Venezuela from Chávez onwards, Hungary under Fidesz, and Turkey after 2014 are widely studied examples.

The distinction from older authoritarianism matters because hybrid regimes use the language of democracy to legitimate themselves. Staged elections, packaged courts, and captured media perform the symbolism of democratic accountability while removing its substance. The annual V-Dem and Freedom House indices trace global trends; both reported a steady drift from full democracy into the hybrid gray zone over the 2010s and early 2020s. Whether that trend reverses, deepens, or simply shifts geographically is still an open question.

title: Federalism & Unitary States
description: Vertical distribution of power: federalism, devolution, and centralization

concepts.title: Unitary, Federal, and Confederal States
concepts.contentHtml:
Every state has to choose where, in the vertical structure of government, real authority sits. The basic typology runs from unitary through federal to confederal, with shades in between.

In a unitary state (France, Japan, the UK in formal terms, China), sovereignty rests entirely with the central government. Subnational units (départements, prefectures, counties) exist by central statute and can be reorganized, defunded, or abolished by central decision. Most countries in the world are unitary.

In a federal state (USA, Germany, India, Brazil, Australia, Canada), constitutionally entrenched powers are divided between national and subnational governments such that neither can unilaterally alter the other's core competences. The 50 US states, the 16 German Länder, and India's 28 states each have constitutionally protected legislative and (often) judicial spheres. Federalism is a constitutional commitment, not just an administrative arrangement.

A confederation (the early United States under the Articles, the modern European Union in important respects) is looser still: subnational units are sovereign and delegate specific powers to a center that depends on them. Most historical confederations have either dissolved or evolved into federations.

concepts.title: Why Federalism?
concepts.contentHtml:
Federalism solves a recurring problem: how to govern a polity too large or too diverse for a single center. The American framers chose it in 1787 to bind together thirteen ex-colonies that would not surrender to one another's full authority. Switzerland, India, Canada, Brazil, Belgium, and Spain (in its "state of autonomies") made similar choices for similar reasons. The European Union is the most ambitious modern attempt to federalize across nation-states, with mixed and contested success.

The case for federalism rests on several claims. It can accommodate diversity (linguistic, religious, ethnic) by letting subgroups govern themselves on the matters they care most about. It can serve as laboratories of democracy (Justice Louis Brandeis's phrase): policies tested in one state and copied if they work, abandoned if they don't. It can check central power by giving subnational governments resources to resist tyranny. And it can match policy to local conditions, since urban Mumbai needs different rules than rural Bihar.

The costs are real. Federalism produces fragmented authority in crises (early Covid-19 responses across US states and German Länder were uneven and sometimes contradictory). It can entrench inequality when wealthy regions provide better services than poor ones. And it can slow national reform by giving subnational vetoes: the US Senate, with two senators per state regardless of population, is a notorious example.

concepts.title: Devolution and the Centralization–Decentralization Spectrum
concepts.contentHtml:
Most real systems sit on a spectrum, not at the corners. Decentralization can be administrative (delegating to local offices), fiscal (granting subnational tax authority), or political (creating elected subnational governments).

The UK is a useful case. Constitutionally a unitary state, it has devolved substantial authority to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland through legislation since 1998, but Westminster retains the legal authority to revoke or alter that devolution, as the 2016 Scotland Act, the 2023 blocking of a Scottish gender-recognition bill, and Brexit demonstrated in different ways. Spain's 17 autonomous communities (especially Catalonia and the Basque Country) operate with extensive self-government inside what is formally a unitary state, in tensions that have repeatedly tested the constitution.

The cross-cutting question for any system is the fiscal compact: how revenues are raised and shared between levels. Subnational units that depend on central transfers tend, in practice, to follow central priorities; subnational units that raise their own revenue have more autonomy and more inequality between them. The German Länder, the Indian states, the US states, and the Spanish autonomies all illustrate different settlements of the same underlying problem.

title: Electoral Systems
description: FPTP, proportional, mixed-member: how vote-counting shapes politics

concepts.title: Plurality and Majoritarian Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest way to count votes is also the most common in the English-speaking world: first-past-the-post (FPTP), in which the country is divided into single-member districts and the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily a majority, wins each seat. The UK House of Commons, the US House of Representatives, the Indian Lok Sabha, and Canada's federal Parliament all use FPTP.

FPTP has predictable effects. Duverger's law (Maurice Duverger, 1951) holds that single-member plurality systems tend toward two-party competition, because votes for third parties are wasted in the sense that they do not translate into seats. The system is disproportional: in the 2015 UK election, UKIP won 12.6% of the vote and 1 seat (0.15% of the Commons); the SNP won 4.7% of the vote and 56 seats (8.6%). Defenders argue FPTP delivers strong single-party governments with clear accountability; critics call it minoritarian rule with millions of unrepresented voters.

Variants include two-round systems (used in French presidential and many legislative elections), where a runoff produces a winner with majority support, and alternative vote / ranked-choice (Australian House, several US states and cities), where voters rank candidates and lower preferences are redistributed until someone clears 50%. Both variants soften some of FPTP's pathologies but retain its single-member-district logic.

concepts.title: Proportional Representation
concepts.contentHtml:
Most established democracies (Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Spain, Brazil, Israel, South Africa) use some form of proportional representation (PR). The principle is that a party's share of seats should approximate its share of votes.

In list PR (Netherlands, Sweden, Israel, South Africa, much of Latin America), voters choose between party lists in multi-member districts; seats are allocated using mathematical formulas (D'Hondt, Sainte-Laguë, largest remainder) to make the seat distribution roughly proportional. Lists may be closed (the party fixes the order of candidates) or open (voters can promote individual candidates within a list).

PR systems typically produce multi-party legislatures and coalition governments. They are more proportional than FPTP, with smaller and more diverse parties represented; minority and regional voices that FPTP filters out tend to get seats. The trade-offs are well known: government formation can take months (Belgium has held world records), and small kingmaker parties can extract concessions out of proportion to their support. Electoral thresholds (a 5% national threshold in Germany, a 3.25% threshold in Israel) are designed to keep micro-parties out without breaking the underlying proportionality.

concepts.title: Mixed Systems and the Politics of Reform
concepts.contentHtml:
Mixed-member systems try to combine the local accountability of single-member districts with the proportionality of PR. Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP), used in Germany, New Zealand (since 1996), and Scotland and Wales, gives each voter two votes (one for a constituency MP, one for a party) and adjusts the party-list seats so the overall result is proportional. Parallel or mixed-member majoritarian (Japan, South Korea, Russia) combines the two tiers but does not compensate, producing a less proportional result.

Electoral reform is itself a political question. New Zealand switched from FPTP to MMP after a 1993 referendum following decades of frustration with disproportional outcomes; Italy has lurched between PR, mixed, and majoritarian-bonus systems multiple times since 1993; the UK rejected the alternative vote in a 2011 referendum. The political scientist Arend Lijphart argued in Patterns of Democracy (1999) that PR and parliamentary systems together produce a more consensus-style democracy, while FPTP and presidentialism produce majoritarian democracy, and that consensus systems perform at least as well on most measures of democratic quality.

Electoral systems are never neutral. They reward some kinds of political mobilization and penalize others.

title: Gerrymandering
description: Packing, cracking, wasted votes, and who gets to draw the lines

concepts.title: Packing and Cracking
concepts.contentHtml:
Where a legislature is elected from single-member districts, someone has to draw the districts, and whoever draws them can decide much of the result in advance. Doing that on purpose is gerrymandering. The word dates from 1812. On February 11 that year, Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry signed a redistricting act that heavily favored his own party.1 One of its new state senate districts, in Essex County, was so contorted that cartoonists drew it as a winged monster,2 and the Boston Gazette printed the cartoon on March 26 as the Gerry-mander.3

The craft comes down to two moves. Packing crams the other side's voters into as few districts as possible, where they win by huge margins.4 Cracking splits the rest among many districts, where they narrowly lose.5 Both manufacture wasted votes: votes cast for a losing candidate, or for a winner beyond what they needed to prevail.6

Small numbers show how far this goes. Take 49 voters, 25 Blue and 24 Red, electing 7 representatives from 7 districts of 7 voters each. A map drawn by Blue can win 6 seats to 1: six districts that Blue carries 4 to 3, with Red's remaining voters packed into one. A map drawn by Red, with exactly the same voters, can win 6 to 1 the other way: Blue's city packed into a single district it wins 7 to 0, and Blue losing every other district 3 to 4. Both maps give every district the same population, and both look tidy. The Gerrymander lab lets you draw them.

concepts.title: Measuring a Rigged Map
concepts.contentHtml:
Courts and reformers have long looked for a test that separates a gerrymander from an ordinary map. The oldest test is shape: a district that snakes across a state looks suspicious. Shape is a weak signal, though. Coastlines, rivers and county lines make honest districts irregular, and a careful mapmaker can rig a map out of compact blocks.

In 2015 the legal scholar Nicholas Stephanopoulos and the political scientist Eric McGhee proposed the efficiency gap: the difference between the two parties' wasted votes, divided by the total number of votes cast.1 A map that makes one party waste far more votes than the other is doing that party's packing and cracking for it. They suggested a gap of more than 8 percent for a state house plan, or two seats for a congressional plan, should make a map presumptively unconstitutional, provided the gap was likely to last the decade.2

Not every skew is deliberate. Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden showed that in many states Democrats are inefficiently concentrated in cities, so they can expect to win fewer than half the seats with half the votes even when nobody draws the lines for advantage.3 Geography packs them by itself.

To separate intent from geography, analysts now have computers draw thousands of alternative maps that follow the same legal rules, then ask whether the real map is an outlier among them. In 2018 Pennsylvania's Supreme Court struck down the state's congressional map after Chen compared it with 1,000 simulated plans4 and found it an extreme outlier for partisan bias that political geography and the districting rules could not explain.5

concepts.title: Who Holds the Pen
concepts.contentHtml:
In most US states the legislature redraws congressional and state legislative districts after each census, so the party in power draws its own seats. The Supreme Court set the first limits in 1964, requiring districts of equal population for Congress1 and for both houses of every state legislature: "Legislators represent people, not trees or acres."2

Partisan gerrymanders proved harder to police. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) the Court held, 5 to 4, that partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts.3 State courts can still strike maps down under state constitutions, as Pennsylvania's did. Race is treated differently, under the Voting Rights Act. In Allen v. Milligan (2023) the Court upheld a ruling that Alabama's map violated the Act,4 but in Louisiana v. Callais (2026) a 6 to 3 majority narrowed it to cases where the evidence supports a strong inference that a state drew its districts intentionally to give minority voters less opportunity.5

The main reform is to take the pen away from legislators. Arizona's voters gave redistricting to an independent commission, and the Supreme Court upheld their power to do so in 2015.6 California's voters created a citizens' commission in 20087 and handed it the congressional maps in 2010.8 Britain and Canada settled the question long ago. Britain's constituencies are reviewed by independent Boundary Commissions, with no direct input from ministers,9 and Canada gave its boundaries to non-partisan commissions in 1964.10

Where the pen stayed partisan, a gerrymander could entrench a minority for decades. In Derry (Londonderry), Northern Ireland, 60 percent of adults were Catholic, yet Unionists held 60 percent of the council seats,11 and a 1969 inquiry found that the ward boundaries had produced a permanent Unionist majority.12

In the United States the fight flared again in 2025. That August, Texas redrew its US House map in the middle of the decade, with districts designed to give Republicans five more seats.13 California answered in November: voters approved Proposition 50, replacing the commission's maps with ones drawn by the Democratic legislature, a shot at as many as five more Democratic seats.14 Several other states followed with new maps, among them North Carolina15 and Florida.16 Whoever holds the pen, the arithmetic is the same: identical voters can elect very different legislatures.

title: Party Systems & Coalitions
description: Two-party, multi-party, dominant-party: Duverger's law and beyond

concepts.title: What Parties Do, and How Systems Are Classified
concepts.contentHtml:
Political parties are the structural intermediaries between voters and governments. E. E. Schattschneider's much-cited verdict, "modern democracy is unthinkable save in terms of parties", captures the consensus: organized parties recruit candidates, structure choice on the ballot, aggregate scattered preferences into governing programs, and provide the durable machinery that elections alone cannot.

The most influential typology of party systems is Giovanni Sartori's (Parties and Party Systems, 1976), which classifies systems by the number of relevant parties and the ideological distance between them. Sartori distinguishes:

  • Two-party systems (US, Britain in the 20th century): two parties dominate, alternation is normal, ideology is moderate.
  • Moderate multi-party systems (Germany, Sweden, Netherlands): three to five major parties, coalitions standard, centripetal competition.
  • Polarized multi-party systems (Weimar Germany, Italy in the First Republic): six or more relevant parties spread across a wide ideological field, with significant anti-system parties at the extremes.
  • Dominant-party systems (Mexico's PRI 1929–2000, Japan's LDP since 1955 with brief interruptions, India's Congress for most of 1947–1989): elections are competitive but a single party reliably wins.

concepts.title: Cleavages, Realignment, and the Decline of Mass Parties
concepts.contentHtml:
Parties do not appear at random. Lipset and Rokkan's influential 1967 essay argued that European party systems were "frozen" reflections of the cleavages produced by two great transformations: the national revolution (center vs periphery, state vs church) and the industrial revolution (urban vs rural, owner vs worker). Most European parties of the mid-20th century mapped onto one or another of these cleavages.

The lock did not last. Realignment, durable shifts in which voters belong to which coalition, has reshaped party systems repeatedly. The post-1968 era saw the rise of postmaterialist politics (Greens, libertarians, identity politics) cutting across the old class cleavage. The 1980s and 1990s saw social-democratic parties move toward the center. Since the 2008 financial crisis and the 2015 European refugee crisis, a populist realignment (radical-right parties in Europe, the Trump-era Republican coalition in the US, AMLO's Morena in Mexico) has scrambled long-stable patterns again.

Across democracies, the long-run trend is the decline of the mass party. Membership in major European parties has fallen by 70–90% since the 1960s; party identification in the US has weakened; voters move between parties more freely. Political scientist Peter Mair argued (Ruling the Void, 2013) that this hollowing of party organizations leaves modern democracies poorly intermediated: visible most acutely in the volatility, fragmentation, and personalized politics of recent elections.

concepts.title: Coalition Formation and Government Stability
concepts.contentHtml:
Most democracies do not produce single-party majorities. Coalitions (formal agreements between parties to govern jointly, usually after an election) are the normal mode of government in PR systems and a recurring feature of FPTP systems too (the UK had coalitions in 1915–1922, 1931–1945, and 2010–2015).

Two ideas structure most coalition theory. Minimal-winning coalitions (William Riker, 1962) are the smallest combinations that command a majority: the prediction is that parties prefer them, since adding redundant partners means sharing offices and policy concessions for no extra parliamentary security. Connected coalitions (Robert Axelrod, 1970) add ideological proximity: parties prefer to coalition with neighbors on the political spectrum, since policy distance is itself costly.

Real coalition formation is messier. The German "traffic-light" coalition (SPD–Greens–FDP, 2021–2024) crossed three colors and broke before its term. Belgium famously took 541 days to form a government in 2010–2011 and broke its own record in 2018–2020. Coalition agreements, written multi-page treaties spelling out portfolios and policy commitments, are now standard in Germany, the Netherlands, the Nordic countries, and increasingly elsewhere. Coalition discipline depends on these agreements, on the parties' continued mutual interest, and on the structural incentives the electoral system provides.

title: State Capacity & Failed States
description: Weberian legitimacy, monopoly on violence, public goods, when states collapse

concepts.title: What State Capacity Is
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential modern definition of the state is Max Weber's, in his 1919 lecture Politik als Beruf ("Politics as a Vocation"): the state is "a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory." The Weberian state is built on three claims (territory, force, legitimacy) and each can fail independently.

Modern political science has expanded this into the concept of state capacity: the bundle of capacities a state needs to actually do what it claims to do. The political economists Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, together with the historical sociologist Charles Tilly, have helped formalize three components.

  • Coercive capacity: a functioning army and police that the center actually controls. Without it, warlords and militias fill the vacuum.
  • Fiscal capacity: the ability to assess and collect taxes. Tilly's famous slogan, "war made the state and the state made war," captures the historical link: European states built tax bureaucracies because they needed to fund wars.
  • Administrative capacity: the courts, bureaucracies, schools, and hospitals that deliver routine governance. Without competent administration, even policies that pass into law do not become real.

State capacity matters because almost every other political outcome (economic growth, democratic stability, public health, security) depends on it. Democracy without capacity produces unstable populism; capacity without democracy produces durable authoritarianism. The two need to be analyzed together.

concepts.title: Failed and Fragile States
concepts.contentHtml:
A state "fails" when it loses one or more of its core capacities so completely that it can no longer perform the basic functions assumed in international politics, keeping the peace, raising taxes, providing courts. The political scientist Robert Rotberg's When States Fail (2004) and the annual Fragile States Index (Fund for Peace) try to map the spectrum.

Failure is rarely a single event. Somalia after 1991 is the clearest case: central government collapsed, Mogadishu split between militias, and the international Transitional Federal Government and its successors held only fragments of territory while al-Shabaab and clan factions held others. Libya after 2011 fell into a similar pattern of competing governments. Yemen since 2014 illustrates a slower failure under sustained civil war and external intervention.

Most fragile states sit on a less dramatic spectrum. Haiti's recurring breakdowns, South Sudan's post-independence civil war, the long instability in eastern DR Congo, and the chronic weakness of central authority in much of Sahelian Africa all illustrate states that retain formal sovereignty but lack the capacity to enforce it. Failure is also reversible: Rwanda after 1994 and Liberia after 2003 are cases of post-conflict states rebuilding administrative capacity, even if at significant cost in pluralism.

concepts.title: The Building of Capacity: Tilly, Fukuyama, and Why It's Hard
concepts.contentHtml:
The historical literature on how states get built is dominated by Charles Tilly (Coercion, Capital, and European States, 1990). Tilly's argument: early modern European rulers needed money to fight constant wars; they built tax-collecting bureaucracies, courts, and standing armies to extract that money; and the state apparatus that emerged then governed for everything else. The fiscal-military state is the historical core of modern governance.

Francis Fukuyama's two-volume history (The Origins of Political Order, 2011; Political Order and Political Decay, 2014) generalized the picture. A modern political order, he argued, requires three components (a strong state, the rule of law that constrains it, and democratic accountability that contests it) and the historical sequence in which they arrive matters. England got rule of law before mass democracy; Germany got a strong state before either; the United States got democracy before strong administrative capacity. The order produces different durable pathologies in each case.

The hardest contemporary policy question is whether state capacity can be built from outside. Two decades of post-Cold War interventions (Bosnia, Afghanistan, Iraq, South Sudan) produced very mixed results. The combination of long timelines, local-elite incentives that often run against capacity-building, and the difficulty of imposing legitimacy from above makes external state-building one of the genuinely difficult problems in contemporary international politics. The pessimistic conclusion of much recent scholarship (Acemoglu and Robinson's The Narrow Corridor, 2019) is that capacity has to be built endogenously, in tension with society, by a domestic process no outside actor can reliably accelerate.
